messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 67

# Marcus

Marcus is a fifty-five-year-old painter who has spent the last thirty years transforming spaces with color and precision. His hands know the weight of a brush, the rhythm of a roller, the discipline required to cut a perfect line. He takes pride in his work—the way he can visualize a room's potential and bring it to life. His wife, Amara, often teases him about how he notices the paint on every wall they pass, assessing quality and technique like other people read newspapers.

Eighteen months ago, Marcus's youngest son, David, died suddenly of a heart attack. David was thirty-two, a healthy man with a wife and two young children. There had been no warning, no illness, no time to prepare. Marcus was at a job site when he received the call. He remembers standing in an unfinished living room, roller in hand, the afternoon light streaming through bare windows, when everything became unreal.

The funeral happened in a blur. Marcus moved through it mechanically, speaking to relatives, accepting condolences, his body present but his mind somewhere else entirely. He returned to work two weeks later because staying home felt worse. The empty house amplified the silence.

But something has shifted in the months since. Marcus finds himself unable to concentrate on jobs that once brought him satisfaction. He'll be painting a bedroom, and suddenly his chest tightens. His breathing becomes shallow. He sets down his brush and has to sit, sometimes for an hour, waiting for the sensation to pass. He's started making mistakes—missed spots, uneven coverage—things that never happened before. His clients have noticed. One asked if he was feeling alright.

At night, Marcus lies awake beside Amara, his mind replaying moments he wasn't even present for. He imagines David's final moments, the confusion, the fear. He wonders if David called out for someone. He wonders if it hurt. These thoughts come uninvited, vivid and relentless, usually between two and four in the morning. When he does sleep, he sometimes wakes gasping, his heart racing as if it's his own body betraying him.

Crowds have become difficult. A trip to the hardware store can leave him feeling exposed and panicked. He avoids his usual suppliers, preferring to order online. He's stopped attending his weekly poker game with friends. Amara invited her sister to visit last month, and Marcus found himself irritable and withdrawn, unable to engage in normal conversation. He apologized afterward, but the effort of being around people feels monumental.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt. He was not there when David needed him. He was painting someone else's walls. This thought loops endlessly. He knows intellectually that he couldn't have prevented anything, but the knowledge doesn't penetrate the feeling. He's also angry—at his body for surviving, at God or fate or whatever took his son, at the randomness of a heart that simply stopped.

Amara has suggested he talk to someone. She's worried about him. He's lost weight. He drinks more than he used to. The house where he and Amara have built their life together now feels like a place where something essential is missing. He walks past David's old bedroom sometimes and cannot bring himself to open the door.

Marcus still goes to work. His hands still know what to do. But the joy has drained from it, leaving only the mechanical repetition of a man trying to paint over something that cannot be covered.
